bio.en: Julie Zhuo is the co-founder and President of Sundial, a leadership and AI tooling company, and previously spent 13 years at Facebook rising from designer to VP of Product Design.
bio.zh: 朱莉·卓（Julie Zhuo）是 Sundial 公司的联合创始人兼总裁，该公司专注于领导力与 AI 工具；她此前在 Facebook 工作了 13 年，从设计师一路晋升为产品设计副总裁。

summary.en: Julie argues that AI is dissolving traditional role boundaries, turning everyone into generalist "builders" who can do many jobs themselves. She describes modern management as being sturdy while staying flexible, like a willow tree that survives storms. The conversation explores how managers should adapt as the rate of change accelerates and models become core resources.
summary.zh: 朱莉认为，AI 正在消解传统的角色边界，让每个人都变成能做多种工作的通才型"构建者"。她把现代管理形容为"柔中带刚"——像柳树一样既能挺过风暴又保持灵活。本期探讨了在变化速度加快、模型成为核心资源之际，管理者应如何调整自身。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're seeing this kind of flattening of orgs. Everyone's becoming an IC again.
turns.zh: 我们正目睹组织架构趋于扁平化，每个人都又回到了"独立贡献者"（IC）的角色。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: It used to be, okay, I don't have the skills to do 10 different jobs, but now with AI allows me to do many of those jobs myself. We need to dissolve the boundaries of these traditional roles and call ourselves builders. I'd love for us to get to the world where that's the title.
turns.zh: 过去，人们会说"我没有能力同时胜任十种不同的工作"，但现在借助人工智能，我们可以自己完成许多此类任务。我们需要打破传统角色的界限，称自己为"构建者"。我希望我们能在未来实现这样的目标——让"构建者"成为职场标配。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also just saw a stat Google let go of so many of their middle managers.
turns.zh: 我刚看到一则数据，谷歌裁掉了大量中层管理人员。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Management is still really critical. You have a north star, you have a vision, and you're just trying to figure out how to use the resources that you have to get that thing done. Used to be people, but now it's basically models and different models have different strengths. You have to assemble the Avengers so that you can use the right tools for the right purposes.
turns.zh: 管理工作依然至关重要。你需要有明确的方向和愿景，然后想办法利用现有资源实现目标。过去靠的是人力，但现在主要依赖模型——不同模型各有优势。你得像组建复仇者联盟般整合资源，确保工具与任务完美适配。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you feel is the biggest change in the role in life of a manager these days?
turns.zh: 你认为当今管理者角色最大的变化是什么？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: It's always been manager's job to manage change. I just think the rate of change is accelerating. Today management is really about this idea of be sturdy while being flexible. So I think about this metaphor a lot of the willow tree. It can survive a lot of storms, disasters, et cetera, but it's also very flexible.
turns.zh: 管理者向来肩负着驾驭变革的重任。但如今变革的速度正在加快。我认为管理的核心理念是"在保持灵活性的同时保持稳固"。为此我常以柳树为喻——它能抵御诸多风雨灾害，同时又极具韧性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have such an interesting trajectory from being head of design to now being obsessed with data and analytics.
turns.zh: 你从设计主管到如今专注数据与分析，职业发展轨迹令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: You want to diagnose with data and treat with design. Data is not a tool that's going to tell you what you should build. I don't actually think a lot of the fast growing companies are using data well at this point. Traditionally things just didn't grow that fast. These companies are totally getting by on just good instincts and good vibes, but what always happens is eventually things stop growing.
turns.zh: 你想用数据诊断问题，再用设计解决方案。数据并非能直接告诉你该开发什么功能的工具。说实话，我觉得很多快速成长的公司目前并没有善用数据。传统上，企业发展速度没这么快。这些公司完全靠直觉和良好感觉支撑，但最终总会遇到增长停滞的困境。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I 100% believe that and agree with that, which is that management is just about, in my mind, having an outcome. So you want to get something done. That's the thing. You have a north star, you have a vision, and you're just trying to figure out how to use the resources that you have to get that thing done. And typically when we talk about management in traditional settings, we talk about the resources being people, and getting the right talent, and making sure that you've got the assemble the Avengers, so you've got the right mix of skills that you need. And then the third thing is process, which is how should all of these different people and tools come together? (00:10:07): And these are still the fundamentals of working with agentic systems. 我完全认同这一观点：在我看来，管理的核心就是达成目标。所以你要确保事情能顺利完成。这才是关键所在。你需要有一个北极星般的愿景，明确目标，然后想办法利用现有资源来实现目标。传统管理观念中，资源通常指人力资源，即如何组建一支高效的团队，确保人才组合合理，形成合力。

第二个关键点是目标设定。所有成员是否清楚如何发挥才能？我们是否有明确的目标和使命？第三个要素是流程设计，即如何让各类资源和工具有效协同。（00:10:07）这些依然是与智能系统协作的基本原则。你必须设定清晰的目标，理解不同模型的优势（如今这些模型已从传统的人力转向智能算法），理解不同模型的个性特质，从而精准匹配工具与场景。此外，你还需要持续评估智能模型的表现，确保在高难度任务中高效运作。

（00:10:59）归根结底，核心原则始终如一。我完全赞同你的观点，即未来我们将越来越需要强化这些管理技能，才能有效应用AI工具。

You have this list of a manager's job is to build a team that works well together, support members in reaching their career goals and create processes to get work done smoothly and efficiently, which is basically exactly what you just said. Interestingly, that middle bullet is the part you don't have to worry about anymore with agents. You don't have to worry about their career development and progress in [inaudible 00:11:29]
turns.zh: 基于此，我带来了你的书籍。书中列举了管理者的三大职责：组建高效团队、支持成员实现职业目标，以及建立顺畅高效的工作流程。这与你刚才的论述完全契合。有趣的是，书中第三条要点——支持成员职业发展——在使用智能模型时已不再适用。我们无需再操心他们的职业成长，至少在短期内如此。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: That's true. That's true, though some people do joke that if we don't treat our agents nice, what's going to happen when AGI comes? And maybe it still might benefit us to be kind.
turns.zh: 确实如此。不过有些人会开玩笑说，如果我们现在不善待智能模型，等通用人工智能（AGI）到来时会怎样？或许善待智能模型对我们仍有益处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm one of those people that says thank you to the Waymo when I leave and just thanks ChatGPT when I'm in voice mode. Just like, "Thank you. That was really helpful." So along these lines, I know there's a lot of ways to go here, but just in terms of skills that are important to a manager, which do you think are most valuable to develop in working with agents in AI systems? I think about things like clarity, communication. Just what comes to mind when you think about here's the things you want to double down on as you're learning to be manager that will also help you be really good at AI tooling and working with agents?
turns.zh: 我就是那种离开时会对Waymo说声“谢谢”，使用语音模式时会对ChatGPT道谢的人。我会说：“谢谢你，真的很有帮助。” 基于此，我知道管理者可以从多个方面提升技能，但在与AI系统中的智能模型合作时，哪些技能最为重要？我认为清晰的沟通和有效的协作至关重要。当你思考如何在学习管理技能的过程中强化这些能力时，它们也会助你成为AI工具和智能模型管理的行家。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: The first is defining the goal and defining the outcome and being really, really crystal clear on what does success look like. If you ask a company to do this, we'll know that this is challenging for humans. I think a lot of times when you talk about why is alignment so difficult at a big company, it often comes down to this question, which is different people may have different pictures of what success looks like. And even if I describe in human words, Lenny, I want to build this product and it's going to be amazing, or this podcast episode, which you asked me, want lots of people to hear it and take away things, that's very general. How do we get even more specific so that we know without question whether we've hit it or not. And this is actually a really, really difficult problem. (00:13:06): It's a difficult question for us because, again, we tend to think very high level. So figuring out how to boil it down so that an agent can really understand what success and failure looks like is a lot of the game. And I think this also relates to things like, well, that's why we have to write evals and that's why they're so important, because they're helping us understand what is the objective criteria. And these days I work in data and my company is all about trying to automate data analysis. And the forever question goes the whole point of data and the whole point of metrics and KPIs is we're trying to put a little bit more of an objective measure or get as crystal clear as possible about what success looks like. And I think it's really an art more than it is like a science, but that's the first thing. I think if you're really unclear about what success looks like, the prompt, you're probably not going to get the most amazing work. I think that's true for managing teams and it's very much true for managing AIs.
turns.zh: 首先，要明确目标和预期结果，对成功的定义必须极其清晰。如果你让一家公司做到这一点，我们知道这对人类来说是个挑战。我认为，当人们谈论大公司为何难以达成战略一致时，往往归结于一个问题——不同的人对成功的定义可能存在差异。即便我用通俗的语言描述，比如“我想开发这款产品，它会非常棒”，或者你提到的播客节目，“希望很多人能收听并从中有所收获”，这些都太笼统了。如何让目标更加具体，从而无需质疑是否达成，这确实是个难题。（00:13:06）：这对我们来说是个难题，因为我们往往思考得过于宏观。因此，如何将其具体化，让人工智能真正理解成功与失败的标准，是关键所在。我认为这也与绩效评估相关，绩效评估之所以重要，正是因为它有助于我们明确客观标准。如今我在数据领域工作，公司致力于自动化数据分析。永恒的难题在于，数据、指标和KPI的核心意义在于，我们试图用更客观的衡量标准，或尽可能清晰地定义成功标准。我认为这更多是门艺术而非科学，但这只是第一层意义。我认为，如果你对成功的定义模糊不清，项目很可能无法产出卓越成果。无论是管理团队还是管理人工智能，这都是千真万确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so let me actually flip this on you and talk about another trend that we're seeing, which is this kind of flattening of orgs, managers being let go. Everyone's becoming an IC again. I just had the CEO of Airtable on the podcast and his whole shtick was that CEOs have to become ICs again. He's coding more than he's ever coded again and his feeling is you have to know what's possible by being in the weeds in order to figure out what your product should be. I also just saw a stat that Google let go of so many of their middle managers of smaller teams. It's just like this flattening trend. So do we even need managers, I guess is one question in the future, and then just thoughts on how this will play out?
turns.zh: 好的，我再反过来问你一个我们观察到的趋势——组织结构扁平化，管理者被裁。每个人又回到了独立贡献者的角色。我刚邀请了Airtable的CEO做客播客，他的核心观点是CEO必须重新成为IC。他现在编程的次数比以往任何时候都多，他认为只有深入了解技术细节，才能确定产品该如何设计。我还看到一则数据，谷歌裁掉了大量中层管理者和小团队成员。这就是扁平化趋势。那么未来我们是否真的需要管理者呢？对此你有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: So I think the real promise and magic of AI that we're seeing in the workplace is that it leads us to each individual is far more empowered. So it used to be, okay, I don't have the skills to do 10 different jobs, so I need to supplement by hiring people to do these jobs. I need someone who's really good at design, I need someone who's really good at coding, I need someone who's really good at data analysis, and then I'll assemble that team. But now with AI and my companion, it's like, wait a second, AI allows me to do many of those jobs myself. Now, I'm not going to do them at what's called the PhD or the highest 1%, 10% level, but if I was at the zero or 10th percentile, it can certainly get me even today very quickly up to the 60th, 70th in terms of what the state of the art is. (00:15:34): And I think that that unlocks so many doors. And so the main thing that I felt so excited about, and this is something I tell my team all the time, is we need to dissolve the boundaries of these traditional roles. So in the past, again, we would have a traditional team, engineers, product manager, designer, researcher, data scientist. And I think now the teams can look more like, well, it's just two people. And they could be any of these traditional disciplines, but the key thing is they can now use AI to help themselves do a lot of the things that the other folks used to be able to do. So in some ways we can drop all of these different role distinctions and call ourselves builders. I think that's sort of the most general purpose way of thinking about what we can all be. We can all be builders. We can all be builders and I'd love for us to get to the world where that's like the title.
turns.zh: 我认为，我们在职场中看到的AI的真正潜力和魔力在于，它让每个人都变得更加强大。过去的情况是，如果我没有能力胜任10种不同的工作，就需要雇佣其他人来完成这些任务。比如，我需要一个设计能力出色的人，一个编程能力强的人，一个数据分析能力高超的人，然后把他们组建成一个团队。但现在有了AI和我的助手，就好像，等等，AI让我自己就能胜任许多这类工作。当然，我不会达到博士级别或最顶尖1%或10%的水平，但如果我处于0%或10%的水平，现在它就能迅速让我达到60%、70%的行业水平。（00:15:34）我认为这为我们打开了许多新的大门。所以最让我兴奋的是，我经常和团队说的一件事是，我们需要打破这些传统角色的界限。过去，我们通常会有一个传统的团队，工程师、产品经理、设计师、研究员、数据科学家。而现在，团队可能只需要两个人。他们可以来自任何这些传统领域，但关键是，他们现在可以利用AI来帮助自己完成过去别人才能做的事情。因此，在某种程度上，我们可以抛开所有这些不同的角色区分，把自己称为建设者。我认为这是一种最通用的思维方式，我们都可以成为建设者。我们都可以成为建设者，我希望我们能在一个这样的世界里生活，那里“建设者”就是一个职位名称。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's funny. That's the term I've been actually using more and more. I used to orient this podcast as a newsletter around product managers and then I started using just product to be a little more broad. And now I'm actually using that term builder and I love that term because it's exactly what you're saying. And this is very much a theme that comes up often in these conversations more and more, just the lines are blurring. I'm curious at your company, how does that look? What are you doing differently? What are you seeing on the ground within your company that maybe would be different from a few years ago?
turns.zh: 这很有趣。这正是我越来越常用的术语。我曾把这个播客定位为面向产品经理的新闻通讯，但后来我开始用更宽泛的“产品”一词。现在我又在用“建设者”这个词，我很喜欢这个词，因为它和你说的一模一样。这也是我们在这些对话中越来越频繁提到的主题，界限正在模糊。我很好奇在你的公司里，情况是怎样的？你们做了哪些不同的尝试？在公司内部，你观察到哪些与几年前相比有所不同的现象？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: So we have eliminated more roles. For example, we thought we would need a bunch of product managers. It's turned out that actually if you don't have a product manager, I know this might be going against a little bit of the ethos of where Lenny started, but I find that sometimes when you have a designer or a product manager, and let's say I'm an engineer, then when I have a problem, like I need to figure out the product definition, my default will be, well, I've got these people and that's kind of their job description, so I'm just going to delegate that to them. And I think that in doing so, again, we want to be polite, we want to respect everyone's lanes. I think that's a missed opportunity for that, if I'm the engineer, to be like, "Wait a second, I should probably focus a lot, too."I need to understand and have an opinion about what to build or what the user experience is. (00:17:54): And so we found that if we actually make teams smaller and we even in the past, pre-AI, just have fewer of these, it allowed everyone to be like, "Wait, we don't have product manager on the team, so communication's up to me. Figuring out how we get greatest value to users is something that is now strictly in my charter. And so that's why I'm such a big fan of we can make teams smaller and we can eliminate these lines. Sure. Again, I'm not trying to say everyone has to do everything. We still can respect the fact that you might be much better at this particular skill than me, but it's less about the role and it's more about the specific context that we're in. (00:18:32): And I find that whenever you have teams and you empower them to be able to take more action on their specific context rather than having these higher level of rules or policies or this is how it's supposed to be, then you get better work. You get faster work and you get happier employees because people feel like they actually can have the power to create the thing that they want.
turns.zh:
因此，我们裁减了更多职位。比如，我们原本以为需要大量产品经理。但事实证明，如果没有产品经理，我知道这可能与伦尼创立公司的理念相违背，但我发现有时候当团队里有设计师或产品经理时，比如我作为工程师，当遇到需要明确产品定义的问题时，人们的默认反应往往是：“反正有这些专人负责，我只需把任务委派给他们。” 我认为这样做未免太不负责任，未能充分发挥每个人的潜力。如果我是工程师，我应该会停下来反思：“等等，我也应该专注于此。”我需要深入理解并形成对产品定义和用户体验的见解。  
（00:17:54）：因此我们发现，如果团队规模更小——甚至在AI时代之前，我们就减少了这类角色——每个人都会意识到：“等一下，我们团队里没有产品经理，所以沟通任务就落到我身上了。如何为用户创造最大价值现在完全是我的职责了。” 这就是为什么我极力主张缩小团队规模，消除这些职能界限。当然，我不是说每个人必须包办所有事务。我们仍然要尊重这样一个事实：你可能比我更擅长某项特定技能，但重点不在于职位头衔，而在于我们所处的具体环境。  
（00:18:32）：我发现只要团队被赋予权力，让他们能根据具体情境采取更多行动，而非受制于高层规则或条条框框，工作成效就会显著提升。工作进度更快，员工也更快乐，因为他们能切实感受到自己有权力去创造理想的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really interesting, just that constraint of not having a PM makes the engineer realize they're not going to wait for someone else to do it. They have to figure it out. The obvious trick there is they have to be good at this. It's a very different job from engineering to be really good at articulating here's the problem we're going to solve, here's why it's important that we're solving, here's how we're going to prioritize everything we're thinking about, here's how we get alignment. Is there something you do differently when you're hiring these engineers, knowing you're going to probably not hire PM? And just that feels really hard to hire for someone that's really good at all these things.
turns.zh:
这真的很有意思。没有产品经理的约束，让工程师意识到他们不能再坐等别人来做决策了。他们必须自己想办法解决问题。关键在于他们必须擅长这项工作。从工程师转变为产品经理，需要具备截然不同的能力——要善于清晰地阐述我们要解决的问题、说明解决问题的意义、规划优先级、达成共识。  
在招聘这类工程师时，如果知道可能不会招聘产品经理，你们会采取哪些不同的策略？要找到一个既擅长工程又精通产品的人实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: It is true and I'm not trying to say again that everyone needs to be good at everything. I don't think that's very realistic. I do think, for example, if we were going to create a team and we're going to have a couple engineers and none of them are very good at thinking through product requirements or what the user angle is, we probably do need to supplement the team with somebody with that skill set. And that might be a designer, or that might be another engineer who's really good at that, or that might be a traditional product manager, or even sometimes a data analyst who's really good at it. So that skill is still important and the team still needs to have that skill, otherwise it's probably not going to produce the best outcome. But I like to think of it as what are the skills that are needed for this and can we now find a couple people? (00:20:13): But it doesn't mean we just automatically go to that script of need a PM, need a designer, need three engineers, need that. Another example for us is even thinking about front end, back end engineering. And it used to be like some people are front engineers. So if you have a project and it's got some front end, some back end, the shortcut is like I need one of these and one of these and that's how it's going to go. But if you say, look, you're an engineer, you're a builder, this has a little bit of front end, but you know what? You can probably figure that out. Use AI to help you figure it out. Get obviously someone who's a specialist to review the code or to give you some high level guidance on things, but just do it. And ever since we started to implement that as well, we see again a little bit of you have to invest a little bit in the beginning. So people are not as comfortable. (00:21:01): They have to learn, so initially things take longer, takes a little bit of extra time, versus if you did slot in a front-end specialist and this is a front end project. It probably would've gone a little bit shorter, but in the long run that investment really pays off because now you have a lot more people who are, again, a little more well rounded and can take on many more pieces just on their own. And then in specific scenarios this is super front and heavy. Sure, let's still bring in somebody who is more specialized in that particular skill.
turns.zh: 确实，我不想再强调每个人都要样样精通这一点。我觉得这不太现实。比如说，如果我们要组建一个团队，团队里有几个工程师，但他们都不擅长思考产品需求或用户视角，那我们可能就需要引入具备这类技能的人才。可能是设计师，也可能是其他擅长这方面的工程师，甚至是传统的产品经理，有时甚至是数据分析师。所以这些技能仍然很重要，团队仍需具备这些技能，否则可能无法产出最佳成果。但我更倾向于思考：我们需要哪些技能，现在能否找到合适的人才？（00:20:13）但这并不意味着我们要机械地套用“需要产品经理、需要设计师、需要三个工程师”这样的模式。另一个例子是前端和后端工程。过去有些人专门做前端工程。所以如果一个项目既有前端部分又有后端部分，通常的做法是分工明确。但现在我们会说：看，你是个工程师、是个开发者，这个项目有一点前端内容，但你知道吗？你应该能搞定。用AI来辅助你解决问题，让专业人士来审核代码或提供高层指导，但关键是行动起来。从我们开始实践这种模式以来，我们发现前期确实需要投入一些精力。人们会不太适应，需要学习新技能，所以初期效率较低。但从长远来看，这种投入是值得的，因为现在更多员工变得更加全能，能够独立承担更多任务。在特定场景下，比如纯前端项目，引入专业前端工程师固然高效，但如果团队内部就能完成相关工作，效率会更高。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you've had the experience of working at a mega large company at Meta and now you're building your own startup that's small and in the middle of this trend of just staying very small and staying really lean and just everyone doing more things. It's so cool that you're experiencing that. So a couple of questions there, just which functions are you seeing most accelerated with all these AI tools? Is it engineering? Is it something else? And then are there tools that have been most helpful to you? Just AI tools for folks who'd be like, "I should check it out." I'm guessing Cursor, but curious if there's anything else.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你曾在Meta这样的大型公司工作过，现在又在创办自己的初创公司。这家公司规模不大，正顺应当前保持小规模、精简高效的趋势。能亲身经历这种转变真是太棒了。所以我有几个问题：在所有这些AI工具中，哪些功能对工程部门的加速作用最明显？是工程部门吗？还是其他部门？有没有特别有用的工具推荐给那些想尝试的人？我猜可能是Cursor，但想了解还有没有其他工具。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yeah, certainly engineering is one that, I mean, most of our company is engineers, so that's the one that we focused on a bunch. I certainly do see more people also prototyping things. We have two designers, but we also see engineers. We have a team that's called product science, which is this interesting blend of you can think about it as like a forward deployed person who has a lot of data analysis background and is kind of playing a customer success role and also kind of playing a product role. And you see them starting to take on building more prototypes or getting into some of the engineering. And so it's really lovely to see that blend of everyone can do a little bit of everything else and we're all encouraging each other. The other thing that recently we've also been trying to do a lot more is just obviously we say, "Hey, engineer, now you can do analysis." (00:22:59): And their first thing is like, "Oh, I don't really know analysis." This is where ChatGPT comes in. And it's like traditionally we would say, "Well, I have to learn that from a human. I have to ask this person and now I'm going to take a bunch of their time because I want them to explain everything to me." And in fact, I think these days ChatGPT or these other AI tools are better teachers. I find that we tend to maybe not use them quite as much just for the purposes of accelerating our education or even going through something. Sometimes what I'll do is I'll find a curriculum online. And if you take a course, it'll be like this 12 week curriculum and I'll just feed it into ChatGPT and I'll say, "Help me customize a program for me using the ways that I like to learn." (00:23:43): I am a person who really needs examples. I need a lot of explain like I'm five. Give me an analogy. And I know some other people on my team are like, "These examples don't make any sense." We're different types of learners and so the idea of a tool that personalizes learning for each of us really helps us, I think, accelerate and just learn these skills much faster than before. So yes, the tools are great. We can use Cursor, it helps us, it autocompletes, it writes a bunch of things, but the acceleration of learning I think is another maybe underutilized tool in all of our arsenals just because I know whenever I talk to people, we forget. We don't think that, wait, yes, we could be doing that and just sitting down and probably in 30 minutes or an hour learn so much faster than what we used to be able to do before.
turns.zh: 是的，工程部门无疑是我们公司里最重要的部门，因为我们公司的绝大多数员工都是工程师，所以我们在这方面投入了大量精力。我确实注意到越来越多的人开始进行原型设计。我们有两名设计师，但也有不少工程师参与其中。有一个叫做“产品科学”的团队，这个团队很有意思，他们既有数据分析背景，又扮演着客户成功顾问的角色，同时也承担着产品开发的职责。你会看到他们开始参与更多原型设计，甚至涉足工程领域。看到每个人都能跨领域学习，互相支持，真是令人欣慰。最近我们还加大了这方面的努力。比如，我们会对工程师说：“嘿，现在你可以做分析了。”但他们第一反应往往是：“哦，我不太懂分析。” 这时候ChatGPT就能派上用场了。传统方法可能需要人来手把手教，但现在ChatGPT等人工智能工具已经成为更好的老师。我发现人们往往不常使用这些工具来加速学习或掌握新知识。有时我会在线寻找课程，比如那种为期12周的课程，然后把它输入到ChatGPT里，告诉它：“根据我的学习习惯，为我量身定制一个学习计划。” 我就是那种需要例子的人，需要像对五岁孩子那样解释说明。我知道团队里有些人会说：“这些例子根本说不通。” 我们学习风格各不相同，所以能根据个人需求定制学习方案的工具真的能帮助我们更快掌握技能。没错，这些工具很棒。Cursor能自动补全代码，帮我们节省时间，但我认为学习加速才是我们未充分利用的利器，因为每次和别人交流时，我发现大家都容易遗忘，意识不到“哦，原来我们可以这样做”，然后坐下来用30分钟或一小时就能比以前学得快得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such an interesting point. There's these tools that are in the just in time, helping you move faster, but you also need to learn how to do something, some foundational lessons. What's an area that your team did that? What did they work on learning?
turns.zh: 这观点真有意思。这些工具能提供及时帮助，加快进度，但你还是需要学习基础知识。你们团队在这方面做了哪些工作？他们专注于学习哪些内容？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: So I'll give you an example. I was just talking to an engineer this morning and he's written a bunch of these algorithms. So one of the things our company does is we're trying to automate data analysis, so one of the things we have to do is obviously understand the best practices. If there's a type of question ...
turns.zh: 举个例子吧。今天早上我刚和一位工程师聊过，他写了不少算法。我们公司正在努力实现数据分析自动化，所以首先要掌握最佳实践。比如，如果遇到某种类型的分析问题……

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: ... To do is obviously understand the best practices. If there's a type of question, "Hey, what features are really the ones that people pay for?" We need to kind of figure out what is the right analysis to do. And so the engineer was saying to me, "Julie, I feel like I really understand the how. I know the algorithms, I know we do root cause analysis, how we do that. But what I don't really understand is why or when this would be most useful. In what context in a company would this company come up?" Because he's an engineer, he hasn't done that job of being a PM or an executive that asks these types of questions. And that was like the perfect thing where yeah, traditionally you might've asked someone, but this is more general purpose. There's so much resources in the world on the internet about it. This is like the perfect type of question where if you just talk to ChatGPT, it's probably going to give you a much better answer and allow you to go deeper. (00:25:55): And a secondary thing we've been learning too is this idea of, almost like as a... Using ChatGPT it's for to test your learning. So explains a bunch of things. And so what I often like to do is like, "Okay, I read this, so this..." I try to explain back what I heard. "So does this mean... Is that right way to think about it, that this is kind of like this analogy?" And ChatGPT will critique me. "Yes, that is right," or "No, you didn't quite get that right. In fact..." And it always tries to say it nicely. This is a funny part. It'll be like, "That's close, and then eventually it's like, "You were completely wrong." Just in the style. But it helps so much because it's interactive and so we can really test whether we really understand the concept by trying to retell it back in our own way.
turns.zh:
显然，关键在于理解最佳实践。如果遇到这样一个问题："嘿，人们真正愿意为哪些功能付费？"我们就需要找出正确的分析方法。工程师对我说："朱莉，我觉得我已经掌握了技术层面的知识——我了解算法，也知道如何进行根本原因分析，但我不明白为什么或何时这种方法最有用。它在公司的什么场景下最适用？"因为他是工程师，没有担任过产品经理或高管这类需要提出此类问题的角色。这正是一个绝佳的例子，传统上你可能会向他人请教，但现在有了更通用的工具——网上有大量相关资源。像ChatGPT这样的工具能为你提供更优质的答案，让你能更深入地探讨问题。

（00:25:55）：我们还学到了另一个要点：使用ChatGPT其实是在测试自己的学习效果。比如，它会解释很多概念。我常会这样做："好的，我读了这段内容，那么……"然后试着用自己的话解释理解到的内容。"所以这是否意味着……这样思考是否正确？这类比喻是否合适？"ChatGPT会给出评价："是的，没错"，或者"不，你理解得不准确。事实上……"它会用礼貌的方式指出错误。这很有趣，有时它会说："你已经接近正确答案了，但最终还是错了。"但这种互动方式非常有帮助，因为我们可以通过用自己的语言复述来检验是否真正理解了概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's incredible just how many ways all this AI breakthrough is helping us advance and do more and learn more and become better. I know there's some downsides, but this is incredible. So many ways of getting better and faster. I want to spend a little more time on this data analysis stuff. So again, you have such an interesting trajectory from working at a big company to starting your own small company. From being head of design to now being obsessed with data and analytics. So let me spend a little time there. What do AI companies that have kind of figured out how to use AI for data analysis and data work, doing differently, what are people missing and sleeping on in terms of getting better at working with data? And let me just add this point. It feels like we're almost working through , here's all the blockers to a team moving forward. There's like waiting for the PM to write the PRD and then there's waiting for the data scientists to give you answers analysis. So this is another really cool unblock that every team member will have.
turns.zh: 人工智能的突破以如此多样化的方式帮助我们进步、提升效率、获取更多知识、变得更出色，这真是令人惊叹。我知道也有一些弊端，但这实在太棒了。有如此多的改进和加速的机会。我想多花些时间在数据分析方面。所以，再次提及，你从大公司跳槽到创办自己的小公司，经历了从设计主管到专注数据与分析的转变，这条发展轨迹很有趣。让我再深入探讨一下。那些成功利用人工智能进行数据分析和数据工作的公司，在哪些方面做得不同？在数据处理方面，还有哪些被忽视却能显著提升效率的关键点？让我补充一点。这感觉我们几乎正在扫除所有阻碍团队前进的障碍。比如，等产品经理写好PRD，再等数据科学家提供分析结果。这又是一个能让每个团队成员受益的绝佳突破。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: So your first question was how are a bunch of AI companies using data? So the funny thing, my funny answer to this is, I don't actually think a lot of the fast-growing companies are using data well at this point. And the main reason why is because traditionally things just didn't grow that fast. And so if you got to a hundred million users, your company has probably been around for a while, and if your company has been around for a while, you've had time to set up things like logging and you've hired a growth team at that point and you've hired a data team and they've done a bunch of work to log an instrument and then transform the data. And we've talked about what is the observability for our business. And you just usually had years to build and develop that, because of the rate of growth. (00:28:25): And so today we see companies that are growing insane and there's still about 10 people or two people or however many people, but they've got hundreds of millions in ARR and hundreds of millions of users. And you know what? They don't actually have all of that infrastructure, that logging, to be able to truly do data analysis. So I would say that these companies are totally getting by on just good instincts and good vibes and we see that. You don't really need data analysis to sometimes make something that works. But I think what data helps us do is in my mind it sort of is helping us reflect back what is really reality. And so of course if ARR growing, awesome, great, keep doing what you're doing. But what always happens is eventually things stop growing. Growth does not happen forever. And usually when growth stops, everyone has this question of, "What's going on? Why did it happen?". (00:29:22): And then you start to be able to see the power of, if you've instrumented everything very well and you have a very good observability model for your business, it's much easier to start to get into the root cause, it's easier to even predict whether growth will slow down at a certain point, it's easier to catch these trends earlier. If you don't have good observability over how your business runs and what the company's key levers are, then you will be scrambling, and at that point, that's usually when people start investing a ton in data. So I wouldn't say that a lot of these hot companies are quite there yet, but what I also think is a trend is that every time there's a new technological shift, we actually have to change the way that we think about... Analysis has to answer the questions that we have, and if technology changes or context changes, we need new methodologies of analysis. (00:30:16): So for example, when mobile came to the forefront, looking at sessions or sessions per day or time spent on mobile, or length of sessions became something that was important for us to understand, are people getting value in this new medium? I think that's the same with what we have today. Conversational analytics is totally different. Used to be, let's say in the Google world, I knew you were interested in shopping if you click the shopping tab, I know you're interested in maps if you click the maps tab, we can measure clicks. Today it's just all conversation, and so it's actually harder for us to tease apart what is the user intent. (00:30:55): If I worked on any of these LLM, I would say one of probably the biggest questions is, hey, what use cases are growing or what use cases are shrinking? And that's much harder to tell today because it's not just clicks on tabs or pages. It's like we have to probably use an LLM or a machine learning model to bucket user intent. We probably have to ask questions like, is the flow going really well in conversations? Like, if I just ask one question and I don't go back and forth, did the user get value? It's always trying to get back to, we're trying to figure out if this was a good experience, but now it's like we need to actually invent new methodologies to help us analyze that.
turns.zh:
你的第一个问题是，众多AI公司如何利用数据？说个有趣的回答吧，我觉得很多快速增长的公司目前并没有充分利用数据。主要原因是传统上，企业的增长速度没那么快。比如，当你用户数达到1亿时，公司可能已经运营了一段时间。此时，你有时间搭建日志系统，组建增长团队和数据团队，他们会花大量精力记录数据并进行转化。我们还讨论过如何实现业务的可观测性。但由于增长速度缓慢，这些工作通常需要数年时间才能完成。  

如今，我们看到一些公司增长速度惊人，比如用户数达数亿，但他们可能只有10名员工或两名员工，却已实现数亿美元的ARR。问题是，他们没有完善的日志系统来支持数据分析。这些公司主要靠直觉和良好的感觉运作。我们确实见过有些产品仅凭直觉就能成功，但数据分析能帮助我们反思现实。  

当然，ARR增长很棒，但增长终会停滞。增长不可能永续。当增长放缓时，人们总会追问原因。这时，完善的日志系统和可观测性模型能帮助快速锁定问题根源，预测增长放缓趋势，提前发现市场变化。若缺乏业务可观测性，公司只能被动应对，往往这时才开始大规模投资数据分析。  

我认为许多热门公司尚未达到这个阶段，但趋势是，每次技术变革都需要重新审视分析方法。例如，移动时代关注会话数、日均使用时长等指标；而当下对话式分析则完全不同。过去，谷歌系统能通过点击行为识别用户兴趣；如今对话更加复杂，意图解析难度大增。  

若我在LLM团队工作，首要问题是哪些用例在增长，哪些在衰退。这在当下更难判断，因为数据不再局限于页面点击，需要借助LLM或机器学习模型进行深度分析。
关于用户意图的研究。我们可能需要思考一些问题，比如对话流程是否真的顺畅？比如，如果我只问了一个问题，没有进行互动，那用户是否获得了价值？我们始终在追问：这是否是一次良好的体验？但现在，我们需要真正开发新的分析方法来帮助我们解答这些问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think the question is always like with conversation, do you want it to be a long conversation, do you want it to be a short conversation? What's the right answer, what's better?
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这个问题在对话中总是会出现：你希望这是一次长对话，还是短对话？什么才是正确答案，怎样才更好？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had a ChatGPT on the podcast, Nick Turley, and turns out one of the ways they found the most common use cases early on was watching TikTok comments and things going viral on TikTok after they launched. How about that?
turns.zh: 我邀请了ChatGPT的开发者尼克·特利参加播客节目，结果发现，他们早期发现最常见的使用场景之一，就是在产品上线后，观察TikTok评论区的情况，以及那些在TikTok上迅速走红的内容。你们觉得怎么样？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yep, yep
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so I want to come back to this really interesting, unusual path that you took from being a head of design at Facebook, you're an inspiration to so many designers, now you spend your time on a data startup obsessed with data. I don't know, classically designers aren't the biggest fans of experiments and data and making decisions based on data. When you look at designers and you hear designers kind of push back on like, "No, we don't want to be super data driven, we know better than... We have a sense of what's beautiful and great and intuition," all these things, what do you think designers are missing when they feel that and say that when they're afraid of writing experiments and data and kind of want to push that out?
turns.zh: 好的，接下来我想聊聊你从Facebook设计主管转型到如今专注数据创业的这段非凡历程。你对众多设计师来说是个灵感源泉。传统上，设计师并不热衷于实验、数据分析和基于数据做决策。当看到设计师们反驳说：“不，我们不想过度依赖数据，我们比数据更懂……我们有对美感和直觉的判断力”之类的话时，你觉得他们错过了什么？当设计师们抗拒数据实验、排斥数据驱动思维时，他们到底在执着什么？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: There's one phrase that my co-founder and I would always discuss with amongst ourselves very early on in which we shared with a lot of the companies that we work with, which is, what you really want is you want to diagnose with data and treat with design. So data is not a tool that's going to tell you what you should build or what the solution is or how we're going to cure the fact that you don't have really great retention. It's just not. But it can tell you if you have a problem and where that problem or opportunity might be. But you still need to go back and undergo a very creative process to figure out what's the best way to solve that. So that's the first thing I would say, is this framework of, data helps you figure out what's actually happening, what do people like, what are they engaging with, what what not. (00:33:32): It just gives you a story that better reflects reality. Because again, we all have stories. We're like, "Oh, my company's amazing, people love us," blah, blah. That's the story I want to believe, but reality may be a different picture. And so what data is trying to do is capture reality. And by the way, I don't think of data just as it's an AB test and it's quantitative things we can measure. To me data is also, well, what did people put onto TikTok and which things went viral, and what are they saying in the Twitter verse or X verse I guess is what it's called now. (00:34:07): And if you do a customer interview, that's still all data, it's just that that is a little harder to distill and quantify. Although now with AI, we have better tools for synthesizing. So that's all data in my mind and it's just all trying to help us understand what is really happening, what is the phenomenon that's happening in reality and how do we understand it? You still have to go and invent and create and dream, and there's no formula and there's no science that will tell you exactly how you're going to make a hit. You can experiment, which allows you to try more things maybe and more rigorously understand what that does in the short term. It's all very contextualized. A-B tests don't tell you what will happen in the very long run, and again, it's all still data, you still have to synthesize and figure out what to do. (00:34:57): So that's the thing, I'll say. Diagnose with data and treat with design. The second thing I will usually tell designers about, is I find that sometimes, and maybe it's the, let's call it the false precision of numbers that we kind of fall into, right? Because it's like, okay, we got these numbers and the numbers go up. It's like no, the fact that you still have to choose which things you look at, is an art, not a science. And your interpretation of if the number went up 5%, is that good, is that not good, is also an interpretation and is an art, not a science. It's just that sometimes I think we can give ourselves this feeling, and I get it, sometimes there's this instinct to want to control things and we want everything to be buttoned up, and we want to know that if we did ABC, everything will be great, our career's going to be awesome, our product's going to rocket ship. (00:35:49): And I think designers are rightly often pushing back and saying, "No, the reality is this stuff is ambiguous and there's uncertainty and we can never know for sure." And I think all that is quite true. So the other thing I would say that I really support is you just actually can't make a really great product by thinking you can A-B test your way into it. So I fundamentally believe that, but I don't think we should throw the baby out with the bathwater. I think there's actually... You know? It's not either or, it's not like data or design. (00:36:18): It's like these are just tools for us to use, and I would say every amazing designer that I've ever met is absolutely obsessed with trying to get a better understanding of reality. They want to know what users really think, they want to know what they're really doing. If they could read every user's minds, that's the thing we would all want as a designer is like, if I could just know what everyone is thinking, feeling every time they used it, my life would be a lot easier, because then I would be able to build better and better things. And so that's what it's trying to help us do. It isn't perfect, no metric is going to tell you whatever we hope that it can in terms of the true certainty and precision, but it doesn't mean we can't use it to better our product development.
turns.zh:
早期，我和我的联合创始人经常讨论一个理念，并将其分享给我们合作的许多公司：你真正需要的是用数据诊断问题，再用设计解决问题。数据并非能直接告诉你该开发什么产品、解决方案是什么，或者如何解决留存率低等问题——它只是告诉你存在问题，以及问题可能出现在哪里。但你仍需回归到创意过程中，才能找到最佳解决方案。这就是我要强调的第一点：数据能帮助你了解实际情况——人们喜欢什么、参与度如何、哪些方面做得不好。（00:33:32）  
 数据只是呈现更贴近现实的故事。因为我们总会自说自话：“我们的公司超棒，用户超爱我们”之类的。但现实可能并非如此。数据的意义在于捕捉真实情况。比如，用户在TikTok上发布的内容是否走红，Twitterverse或Xverse上的用户讨论内容，这些都是数据。客户访谈同样属于数据，只是更难提炼和量化。不过借助AI工具，我们现在能更好地整合这些信息。对我而言，数据就是帮助我们理解现实发生了什么，理解现实中的现象并找到应对之道。你仍需创新、创造和梦想，没有公式或科学定律能告诉你如何打造爆款产品。你可以通过实验来尝试更多可能，短期内更严谨地理解效果。但一切都因情境而异。A/B测试无法预测长期效果，数据仍需综合分析才能行动。  
 接下来，我想强调第二点：用数据诊断问题，通过设计解决问题。对于设计师，我发现他们有时会陷入数字的虚假精确性陷阱。比如数据上升了，就沾沾自喜。但你必须选择关注的指标，这本身就是艺术而非科学。对5%增长的解读——是好是坏——也是主观判断。  
 有些人想用A/B测试控制一切，幻想产品能一飞冲天。这时候设计师会反驳：“现实是模糊不确定的，我们永远无法预知未来。”我完全认同这种观点。真正伟大的产品绝非靠A/B测试就能诞生。这就是为什么我支持：数据诊断问题，设计解决问题。  

---
因噎废食。我觉得实际上……你懂的？这不是非此即彼的选择，不像数据和设计那样非此即彼。（00:36:18）这些不过是我们可以运用的工具而已。我认识的每一位杰出设计师，都痴迷于深入理解现实。他们想知道用户的真实想法，了解用户的真实行为。如果能读懂每个用户的想法，那就是我们设计师梦寐以求的——如果能知道用户每次使用时的所思所感，那我的工作就轻松多了，因为这样我就能设计出越来越好的产品。这正是用户研究试图帮助我们做到的。它并不完美，没有任何指标能提供我们期望的绝对确定性和精确性，但这并不意味着我们不能借助它来优化产品开发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to say exactly what you just said, which is every great designer that I've worked with was obsessed with data in the most leaning into the data, versus designers that are just like, "Nah, I think I'm good, I have a sense of what's right, and why would we let that tell us what to do?" And to your point, it's not going to tell you what to do, it'll tell you where opportunities arise. Let me take us back to the management chat and maybe just let me ask something broad. What do you feel is the biggest change in the role and day-to-day work and life of a manager these days with the rise of AI?
turns.zh: 我本来想说你刚刚提到的观点——我合作过的每位优秀设计师都痴迷于数据，深深依赖数据；而有些设计师则会说：“不，我觉得我已经很懂了，凭直觉就能判断该怎么做。”正如你所言，数据并不会直接告诉你该怎么做，但它会指明机会所在。让我回归到管理层的对话主题，或许可以问一个更宏观的问题：随着人工智能兴起，管理者的角色和日常工作生活在当下发生了哪些重大变化？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I think that managing change. It's always been manager's job to manage change, and there's always the chaos of what's going on. I just think the rate of change is accelerating, and we've seen that over the last couple of decades. And so I find that there's just a great deal more uncertainty that people have about things, like where is AI going to be in two years from now? I don't know. Who really knows? And so are we going to have AGI in five years? That kind of changes a lot about the landscape. Not to mention, I think there's quite a lot of fear that many organizations are feeling. It's like if my career has always been in design and now these tools are getting better and better at what I'm doing, then holy shit, what happens to my career and my future? And do I need to pivot? Do I need to learn different things? (00:38:25): And so it's this change, it's this feeling of uncertainty. And I think a lot of times managers have to deal with that in addition to what you were saying before, which is they also have to learn these new skills, which is managing AI and managing these more powerful tools in their arsenal of trying to get things done. So that is very different, I think, than maybe 10, 20, 30 years ago. And so I think that the skills that become more important are obviously communication, feedback, compassion, but just being able to work with humans and to have them understand that yes, we are in a state of change. I think every leader has to do this now, every startup founder that I know, every CEO, is how do you land this message that things are changing and we need to be very open to change? (00:39:16): If we go and stick to our old ways, we're probably going to get left behind, our product's going to get left behind, even our way of doing things is going to be left behind. So we need to change. We need to change our product and we need to change the way that we work, as we all talked about in terms of smaller teams, more nimble, blah, blah, blah. But at the same time it's like, how do we do that in a way that doesn't just freak everyone out? And it's like, "Ah, it's chaos. Everything's changing.". (00:39:44): So I think about this metaphor a lot, of the willow tree, which is the willow tree is a very sturdy tree. It can survive a lot of storms, disasters, et cetera, but it's also very flexible. The branches are very, very flexible, and that's in some ways what allows it to be very sturdy. So I think today, management is really about this idea of be sturdy while being flexible, and that is a very hard thing to pull off, but I think that's at least when I even go into... I'm like, "Be like the willow tree, Julie. Just imagine the willow tree and try and channel that as the kind of feeling of what it is that we're trying to do together."
turns.zh: 我认为管理变革始终是管理者的职责，而变革带来的混乱也从未停歇。但近几十年来，变革的速度明显加快。因此，我发现人们对未来充满更多不确定性。比如，人工智能两年后会发展到何种程度？谁又能预测得清？五年内我们会迎来通用人工智能吗？这些变化彻底重塑了行业格局。更令人担忧的是，许多组织正深陷恐惧情绪。比如，如果我一直从事设计工作，现在这些工具却在不断超越我的能力范围，那么我的职业生涯和未来该何去何从？我是否需要转行？学习新技能？（00:38:25）这种不确定感，再加上你之前提到的技能挑战，比如掌握人工智能和更强大的工具以完成任务，这与10、20、30年前相比有天壤之别。因此，如今最重要的技能显然是沟通、反馈、同理心，以及让团队理解变革的必要性。（00:39:16）如果我们固守旧有思维，注定会被淘汰——产品会落后，工作方式也会过时。因此，我们必须变革：更新产品，调整工作方式，如小团队协作、敏捷开发等。但关键在于如何在不引发恐慌的情况下推动变革。“啊，一切都在变化，太混乱了！”（00:39:44）我常用柳树作比喻。柳树根系深扎，枝干柔韧，正是这种灵活性赋予了它顽强的生命力。如今的管理工作需要在稳固根基与灵活应变之间找到平衡，这极具挑战性。但至少在实践中，我常提醒自己：“学学柳树吧，朱莉。想象柳树的特质，努力将这种韧性融入我们的团队协作。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of a couple things from other guests. I had Marc Benioff on the podcast and I asked him, "Just how do you deal with all this change? It's like agents now, it was, I don't know, there's AGI coming as you said, just like, "How do you survive through this?" And his advice is just, he's like, "I'm always just like, 'Good. This is great. This is what we want. This is exciting. We have so much opportunity, it's just not boring. We can always reinvent.'" And he's always embracing with "This is good." And just I'll never forget the way he responded to that.
turns.zh: 这让我想起其他嘉宾曾提到的几个观点。比如，我在播客上采访过马克·贝尼奥夫（Marc Benioff）时问他：“面对所有这些变革，你是如何应对的？比如现在代理商的转变，还有人工智能即将到来，你是如何在变革中生存下来的？”他的建议是：“我总是想，‘很好。这很棒。这正是我们想要的。这令人兴奋。我们有太多机会，这一点都不无聊。我们总能重新发明自己。’” 他总是用“这很好”来回应。我永远不会忘记他当时的反应。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I think if you don't think it's good, it's kind of a painful way to live. It'll be very, very difficult over these next. So I do think that all things be equal, lean into it. If you can wake up every day and see it as opportunity and excitement rather than fear, again, they're all flip sides of the same coin, but I think if we can lean more into what could it be, while recognizing that the other side does exist and it's still there. And I think if managers who try to pretend like it isn't there, it's all good, no one's upset, et cetera, there's something also missing about just addressing and being able to be like, yeah, it's hard. Change is hard. We're probably going to get upset. We're going to have some chaos. This is going to happen, but we will work through it because we're going to be flexible and we're going to be able to put our eyes on the big picture of what is possible, which is exciting.
turns.zh: 我认为，如果你不认为这很好，那生活会很痛苦。接下来的日子会非常、非常艰难。所以我确实认为，在其他条件相同的情况下，应该积极拥抱变革。如果你能每天醒来把它视为机遇和兴奋点，而不是恐惧——毕竟两者不过是同一枚硬币的两面——但我认为，如果我们能更专注于可能性，同时承认另一面确实存在，那就更好了。而那些试图假装问题不存在、一切都很好的管理者，或者说他们只会说没事、没人不开心之类的话，这同样是缺乏直面问题、无法坦然面对现实的表现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's another quote that and came up as you were talking. I forget who it was exactly, maybe Kevin Wheal, maybe Mike Krieger. They said that this is the most normal things will be, ever. Like, it will only get weirder. And I think giving people that sense of like, okay, just enjoy this normal, because this is going to be only weirder, is we'll at least give people an expectation, real expectations where things might be going.
turns.zh: 你刚才提到的另一句话让我想起谁说的。我记不清具体是谁了，可能是凯文·惠尔（Kevin Wheal），也可能是迈克·克里格（Mike Krieger）。他们说，这将是未来最正常的事。事情只会变得更奇怪。我认为给人们这样的感觉——好吧，就享受这种正常吧，因为事情只会变得更奇怪——至少能让人们对可能发生的事有所预期，有真实的预期。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a time to be alive.
turns.zh: 活在当下真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: What a time.
turns.zh: 真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let me zoom out even further and chat about... I want to ask you just outside of AI, management in many ways is unchanged. It's still a lot of the same work, managing people, helping them be successful, producing great work. What are just some of the, I'd say most timeless, most important lessons that you think managers, especially new managers still don't totally understand, need to hear more? What are just some that come to mind? And then we'll see where this goes.
turns.zh: 好的，让我再放宽视野聊聊……我想问你，除了人工智能，管理在很多方面其实没有变。还是有很多相同的工作，管理员工、帮助他们成功、产出优质成果。你认为管理者，尤其是新手管理者仍不完全理解、需要更多听取的最永恒、最重要的教训有哪些？你能想到哪些？然后我们再看看能聊到什么程度。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: The first thing that comes to mind is the importance of managing yourself and understanding yourself. This was chapter five of my book. It's called Managing Yourself. In fact, when I wrote it, I kind of wanted it to be chapter one, and then my publisher was like, "Well, maybe you should get into some of the tactical..." People don't necessarily think managing other people or manage a team starts with them, but I really do fundamentally believe this, because I think all of us, of course, like any human being, we have things that we're strong at, we have things that we're weak at. And I am a very big believer that every strength is its own weakness, and every weakness is a strength. (00:43:18): There's no such thing as you're going to somehow get every dimension to be 100%. In fact, I think one of the most interesting concepts or frameworks for myself, and also even, this is also kind of like a data framework concept, is this concept of dimensionality. So what dimensionality means is you're a human being, but we can kind of look at you in infinite dimensions. There is, for example, how good is Lenny at throwing an ax? That's one dimension
turns.zh:
首先想到的是自我管理和自我认知的重要性。这是我书中第五章的主题，书名叫《自我管理》。其实我写这章的时候，本想把它放在第一章，但出版社建议：“或许你该先讲些实用的……” 人们往往不认为管理他人或团队要从自身做起，但我深信这一点——毕竟我们每个人都有擅长之处，也有不足之处。我尤其坚信，每种优势都暗含着弱势，每种弱势也蕴藏着优势。

（00:43:18）：世上根本不存在全能的人。对我而言，最有趣的概念之一——也是数据框架中的重要视角——是维度理论。维度意味着：你是一个完整的人，但我们可以从无数维度去审视你。比如，莱尼（Lenny）扔斧头的本事有多强？这是一个维度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Pretty good.
turns.zh: 相当不错。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: How good is Lenny at being a podcast moderator? Fantastic.
turns.zh: 莱尼做播客主持人的能力如何？非常出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So-so. Okay, thank you.
turns.zh: 马马虎虎吧。好的，谢谢。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: How good is Lenny at doing a zero to one type of project in the AI space? Right? So again, just can think about these as infinite dimensions. And the reality is each of our profiles is very unique, it's like a fingerprint. So for you it's like these are all these areas that you're really great at, much better, like in the top 1%. And then there's some areas where in the top 10%, then there's some areas where you're kind of average, and then there's some dimensions in which you're worse than average compared to other people. And that's just true for all of us. And what I like about that is therefore if you take that as the model, you realize that none of these dimensions are you entirely. So I can make a comment like "Lenny, your ax throwing really could use some improvement." (00:44:48): And ideally you're not like, "Julie is saying I'm a bad person, my identity is at risk," right? Because it's just one dimension of who you are. But what happens sometimes is that we can get very attached to certain dimensions because we start to think that that's who we are. And I think managers can do that, and clearly individuals on their teams. And when that happens, it starts to get very difficult to have, I think more objective conversations about, okay, what can you get better at? What can get worse at? And so I say all this because I think this framework for me at least, and many people that I've talked to, has helped them realize that somebody can give you feedback or you can be maybe not great at certain dimensions, you can have room to improve, and that's not who you are because you are all of these infinite dimensions in one, and none of them is representative of your true worth as an individual. (00:45:42): I'm a big believer that we are all beautiful and worthy, and sure we have all of these skills and we want to improve those skills, but it does not speak to whether we are worthy or not by saying whether we are strong or weak in these skills. And so I think if you can take that and really internalize that, then you can look at yourself a little bit more objectively as a manager, and you can realize that there are areas where you're going to be really strong, there are areas where you have biases, and often they are one and the same. So I'll give an example. People have often told me, I would get this in my performance reviews from managers in the past, like, "Hey Julie, you're really thoughtful. So when you think about something, you have a way to think about it, you've clearly thought about it in depth and you've got these frameworks and all this. That's a great thing.". And then on the flip side, I'll get feedback like, "Well, Julie, you don't really say a lot in a dynamic discussion. You're kind of quiet and you don't really think that quickly on your feet." And what you realize is these are kind of, again two... Because I don't do that and I'm not just off the cuff, that's what allows me to oftentimes be very, very thoughtful, or at least, okay, when I was younger, it's very clear that that particular weakness also very much is speaking to a particular strength, which is I am the kind of person that doesn't always have a snap judgment. I have to really think about it and internalize it and sometimes get to how I feel, and then I can share it and present it in the world. (00:47:18): And so just knowing that about me is supremely helpful. Now doesn't mean of course that I can never get better at this thing, but what I often think about is mastery is where we realize that both of these we can get better at, and what we want to do is just figure out in the context, what makes sense to be. So I got this feedback and I'm like, "Cool, one of the things I need to work on, is figuring out how to be more open in person, how to speak a little bit more clearly in person, maybe say things like, 'I don't know exactly how I feel about it yet, but this is what I'm thinking right now,'" if there's still clear tactics that will allow me to be a more effective team member and to do a better job in the context of what I'm trying to do with my team. (00:48:04): So I've tried to build those skills, but the meta skill is now being able to step back and say, okay, in certain context it is really important that we move fast and we are decisive and we just do something. And even if it's not perfect, we just kind of have to do it. And if I struggle with that, I should realize that that's an area to improve upon. But there are other contexts in which the right thing to do is actually to take a step back and be very thoughtful and to not rush into decisions. (00:48:31): And that's so what I want to get to is not like let's reject this strength or this weakness, but just know that that's where we come from, that naturally, we might be wired in a particular way. Our growth often looks like getting better at doing the opposite, but not rejecting again the thing that we're good at, but rather over time getting to this balance where we can read the context and the situation and know, "Should I lean a little more thoughtful or is this a time where I need to try and be a little more decisive and just share what's on my mind right now?"
turns.zh:
莱尼在人工智能领域做零到一型项目的能力有多强？对吧？所以再说一次，我们可以把这些看作是无限维度的。现实是，我们每个人的个人特质都非常独特，就像指纹一样。对你来说，有些领域你非常擅长，远超平均水平，可能是前1%；有些领域你处于前10%；有些领域你表现平平；还有些领域你甚至比其他人表现更差。这对我们所有人都是如此。我喜欢这种思维模式，因为如果以此为模型，你会意识到这些维度都不是你的全部。因此，我可以说：“莱尼，你的斧头投掷技术真的需要提高。”（00:44:48）理想情况下，你不会想：“朱莉说我是个坏人，身份受到了威胁。”对吧？因为这只是你个性的一个维度。但有时我们会对某些维度过于执着，因为我们开始认为这就是我们的全部。我认为管理者会这样做，他们团队中的成员也会这样。当这种情况发生时，就很难进行更客观的对话，比如：“你能在哪些方面有所提升？”“哪些方面需要改进？”所以我说这些，是因为至少对我自己，以及我交谈过的许多人来说，这个框架帮助他们意识到：别人给你反馈，或者你可能在某些维度上不那么出色，但这并不代表你的真实价值，因为你是一个由无数维度组成的整体，没有一个维度能代表你的全部价值。（00:45:42）我坚信我们每个人都是美好且有价值的，当然我们拥有各种技能，也想不断提升，但这些技能的强弱并不能决定我们的价值。因此，如果你能真正领会这一点，那么作为管理者，你就能更客观地看待自己，也能意识到自己在某些方面会非常出色，而在其他方面可能存在偏见，而这些偏见往往是一体两面的。举个例子。过去，我的经理在绩效评估中常说：“朱莉，你真的很善于思考。当你思考问题时，总能深入剖析，构建框架，这很棒。”而另一方面，我也会收到反馈：“朱莉，你在动态讨论中不怎么发言，比较安静，反应也不够敏捷。” 你会意识到，这些维度是相互关联的……因为我不随口说笑，这恰恰让我能经常深思熟虑，或者至少，我年轻时很清楚，这个弱点也对应着一个优点——我不是总能轻易下判断的人。我必须认真思考、内化这些想法，有时才能表达出来并展现给世界。（00:47:18）因此，了解自己的这些特质非常有帮助。这当然不意味着我永远无法在这方面有所提升，但我常思考的是：精通某项技能意味着我们意识到这两个维度都可以提升，而我们要做的是
只需在上下文中理清，怎样做才最合适。收到这份反馈后，我想：“太好了，我需要改进的地方之一，就是学会在面对面交流时更开朗一些，表达更清晰些。比如可以说：‘我现在还不太确定自己的感受，但这是我当下的想法’。”如果这样能让我成为更高效的团队成员，在与团队合作时更好地完成任务，那当然值得努力。（00:48:04）我一直在努力培养这些技能，但更重要的能力是学会退后一步，冷静分析：在某些情况下，快速决策、果断行动至关重要，即便结果不尽如人意，也必须先行动起来。而当我在这方面遇到困难时，就该意识到这是需要改进的方面。但在另一些情境下，正确的做法反而是暂停思考、深思熟虑，切忌仓促下结论。（00:48:31）所以我的观点不是要否定某种优点或缺点，而是要明白这些特质源于我们的天性。在成长过程中，我们通常会努力做到相反的方向，但并非否定自身的优势，而是逐渐找到平衡点：在判断情境时，要能分辨“是该多思考，还是该大胆表达当下想法？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice that things that we are incredible at and have a downside, and oftentimes the feedback we're getting is something we're not great at, there's a good version of that that people appreciate. And I was going to ask you, and I think you answered most of this, but just when you got this feedback of, "Hey Julie, you're not speaking enough in these meetings, you're not contributing quickly enough," it sounds like, so one option is just like, "Okay, cool, that's me, that's how I am, and I'm just going to solve the problem this other way and then just not going to change anything." What I heard you say is, find opportunities where you want to actually change that behavior, even though it doesn't come naturally in specific situations where things are moving fast. I guess just how far do you recommend people push themselves in things they're not great at, versus leaning further into their strength, let's say?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个观点：我们在某些方面表现出色，但同时也存在短板，而我们得到的反馈往往是关于我们不擅长的方面。但总有一种被人们认可的良好表现方式。我想问你，虽然你已经回答了大部分问题，但当你收到这样的反馈时：“朱莉，你在会议上发言不够多，参与不够积极。”听起来你可能会有两种选择：第一种是说“好吧，那就是我的性格，我不会改变现状，直接用其他方法解决问题”。而你刚才提到，要在特定场景下主动改变这种行为，比如在快节奏的工作环境中。这里我想问的是：对于不擅长的领域，人们应该如何突破自我，还是说应该更充分发挥自己的优势呢？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Oo, I think that's a really great question. So the way I think about it is it's very dependent on what is your goal. So for example, let's say that you are...
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得这是个非常好的问题。我的看法是，这取决于你的目标是什么。比如说，假设你...

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: ... on what is your goal? So for example, let's say that you are... Let's even take, for example, ICs versus managers. I think often about the pathway of an IC, an individual contributor, as wanting to deepen a craft. You love this thing and you just want to get better and better and better at this very specific skill or this craft, right? So think about in our dimension, infinite... It's like you pick a couple dimensions, "I just want these to be... I want to be the top 0.01%," and that's kind of the pathway of extending it as an IC. Now, if that's your high level goal and you're like, "I want to be able..." Let's say your high level goal is, "I want to be able to do this 10 hours a day because I love it and I want to be able to support myself doing it, meaning I get paid and I have a great job, and I want to have a bunch of impact in the world by doing this thing." (00:50:53): So again, you still have goals. Then you have to see, okay, "Does my strategy of just deepening these things, is there a pathway to reach my goals according to that?" (00:51:03): And if there is, awesome. Then if someone's like, "Hey, do you want to be a manager?" (00:51:06): You're like, "Nope, don't need to because these are my goals and this pathway actually allows me to do that." (00:51:13): But if somehow you get to a point where the skill you really want to perfect is not something that may be commercially viable in the world, that's going to somehow allow you to buy the big mansion that you want to buy to support your family, then I think you have to ask yourself, "Okay, so if I just do this, it's not going to cut it. I might actually need to learn some of these other skills in order to be able to fulfill the job that is going to be valuable enough that people are going to pay me a bunch of money at this certain level so that I can afford my mansion." (00:51:43): So I just think it has to go back to, what are your goals? And there are cases in which yes, it'll support your goal to do this and to deepen your craft. And there are cases in which it won't. And I think it's important, it's a very individual question for each person. But what I often think suffering is, is when these things are not aligned. So what you want is the giant mansion and all of that, but you're like, "But I also just want to spend on my time perfecting my egg omelet." (00:52:12): And then, you're just in this tension place, and it's very hard to feel satisfied and fulfilled because you're a little bit like, "Oh, why doesn't the world value my deep egg omelet skills?" (00:52:26): You can [inaudible 00:52:27] egg omelet, you should maybe not do this thing. Or if you want this thing, you may actually need to be better at just egg omelets. Perhaps you need to expand your repertoire of cuisines, and go and build a Michelin star restaurant or something.
turns.zh: 你的目标是什么？举个例子，就拿IC（个人贡献者）和管理者来说吧。我常思考IC的职业发展路径，他们渴望深耕某项技能。你热爱这项技能，只想在某个特定领域或技艺上不断精进。对吧？在我们的维度里，无限的可能性……你可以选定几个维度，比如“我只想成为……前0.01%的顶尖人物”，这就是IC职业发展的路径。假设你的高层目标是：“我要能每天花10小时做这件事，因为我热爱它，还能以此养活自己，获得高薪工作，通过这项技能为世界带来巨大影响。” （00:50:53）所以你仍然有目标。然后你得审视：我深化这些技能的策略，能否达成我的目标？（00:51:03）如果可以，那太棒了。但如果有人问：“嘿，你想当经理吗？” （00:51:06）你可能会说：“不，我不需要，因为这些是我的目标，而且这条路径能让我实现目标。” （00:51:13）但如果某天你发现，你真正想精通的技能在现实中并不可行——比如无法靠它买下你想养家糊口的大豪宅——那你就得问自己：好吧，那条路走不通。我可能需要学习其他技能，才能找到一份高薪工作，支撑起我的豪宅梦。 （00:51:43）所以关键在于，你的目标是什么？有些情况下，深化技艺能支持你的目标；有些情况下则不然。这对每个人都是个性化的问题。但我常觉得痛苦的是，目标与现实不符。比如你既想买大豪宅，又想每天花时间磨练煎蛋卷技艺，这就是矛盾。（00:52:12）这种矛盾会让人难以获得满足感和成就感，因为你会想：“为什么世界不认可我的煎蛋卷技艺？” （00:52:26）如果你热爱煎蛋卷，或许你不该继续这条路；如果你想继续，或许你得先把煎蛋卷技艺练得更精湛。或许你该拓展烹饪领域，创办米其林星级餐厅之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is really good advice. It's not just definitely always work on your weaknesses or don't worry about them, it's if you need to do this thing to achieve this goal that you have, make sure you understand what your goal is. And then is this thing a thing you need to work on? For example, [inaudible 00:52:52] become a VP, you probably need to be really good in big important meetings, and being on the spot, and just not waiting until everything's over and then sharing an email of all your thoughts.
turns.zh: 这真是很棒的建议。不是说一定要一直改进弱项或不去管它们，而是如果你需要做某件事来达成目标，就要确保你清楚自己的目标是什么。然后这件事是你需要改进的吗？比如，要成为VP，你可能需要在重要会议上表现出色，当场应对问题，而不是等会议结束后再发邮件分享你的想法。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. For me, I actually went through a period where I was like, "I do not want to get promoted. I'm so happy in this very specific role, just leave me alone." And that path is very different from the skills I need to build to be a manager. And then things changed and then, okay, now these are the things I need to work on.
turns.zh: 是啊。我自己也曾经历过一段时期，那时我觉得：“我不想升职。我现在这份工作太满足了，就别来打扰我了。” 而这条职业道路与我成为管理者所需培养的技能截然不同。后来情况发生了变化，我才意识到，现在这些技能才是我需要努力提升的。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yeah. I love that you knew that about yourself, because I think it's so easy for a young person to go into their career and everyone is telling them, maybe their whole family has been telling them, "You need to level up, you need to get paid more. You need to get that manager title. You need to get a VP." (00:53:33): And at a certain point, I think sometimes people opt into this without knowing what they're actually signing up for. What are the trade-offs? And is that really what you want to do? Does that really align with your passions? And of course, sometimes we have to... Again, it's a compromise for us, but we get to design. We get to design what are goals and what's the right pathway. And I go back to, usually when people are unhappy, it's because these things are a little bit out of sync. They want this big thing, but they're not actually excited about what it takes to do that thing, and therefore it's just going to be a mismatch.
turns.zh: 是啊。我很欣赏你能清楚认识自己这一点，因为我觉得年轻人在职业生涯初期往往会被各种声音裹挟——家人、朋友都催促他们：“你得晋升啊，要涨薪啊，要当经理啊，要升VP啊。”（00:53:33）但有时候人们会不假思索地顺从这些期望，却不清楚其中的代价。这真的符合你的职业理想吗？这真的能激发你的热情吗？当然，有时候我们不得不妥协，但至少我们能自主规划。只要明确自己的目标和正确的发展路径就好。我发现，当人们对工作不满时，往往是因为期望与现实不符。他们渴望某种高位，但对达成目标所需的努力毫无热情，最终只能适得其反。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And along those lines it sounds like, oh, sure, I can design my life and design my role. But what I find is if you at least first of all know what you'd love and ideally do, and then at least mention that to your manager, it often is a lot more possible than you think.
turns.zh: 说到这，听起来好像“我可以规划自己的生活和职位”很简单。但我的经验是，如果你首先明确自己的热爱所在，并向上级提出这些需求，往往比你想象的要容易得多。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: A hundred percent. I think it's so important to be... We often also have this mental model like, "Oh, our managers are our judge, and they're going to judge me on whether or not I did well, I should get a promotion, I should be fired." (00:54:39): So there's this sometimes fear that people have, but I think in the very best relationships, the manager is like a guide. It's like, look, the manager has a job, and if you understand your manager's job, which is how to get better outcomes from the team, and also you understand what exactly would your manager consider success for the team, it also makes it easier for you to then be like, "Oh, well if I do this project, then that clearly seems like it's a very direct path to creating value for the team. And that also is a kind of project that suits my skills. It's something I'm excited about." You should suggest that to your manager. (00:55:16): But the other is true, right? So you would know that if you actually asked your manager, "What is your job and what do you consider success to be, and what is your greatest hopes and dreams?" (00:55:25): And then you might be able to help your own career and yourself because you would know that context. And conversely, if you say, "Hey, manager, these are my hopes and dreams. This is what I think I'm good at. I really want to get better at this skill. I really want to get that VP promotion, but I don't know what it entails. Can you tell me, what does it take?" (00:55:45): That's a really wonderful conversation as well because then you'll get all of that context, and then you can actually decide whether you want to do it or not. And if you want to, then ask your manager for help, "Okay, if you see opportunities that are going to help me become a better presenter or increase my communication, please tell me." Even better, "If you have feedback for me about communication, I want to hear it, because that's what's going to help me grow in this particular skill." (00:56:11): And so, it becomes this collaborative relationship much more so than this almost adversarial, like I'm trying to get you to give me a promotion, and you're trying to get me to work harder. That is not a very good vibe.
turns.zh: 百分之百。我认为建立这样的信任关系非常重要……我们常常会有这样的思维模式：“哦，我们的经理是评判者，他们会根据我的表现决定是否给我升职，或者是否要解雇我。”（00:54:39）所以有时候人们会心存恐惧，但我认为在最理想的合作关系中，经理应该像一位导师。换句话说，经理的职责是如何让团队取得更好的成果，而你若能理解经理对团队成功的定义，就能更清晰地判断某个项目是否能为团队创造价值，同时也更容易发现自己擅长的领域并为之兴奋。这时你应该向经理提出自己的想法。（00:55:16）但反过来也同样适用，对吧？如果你主动问经理：“你的职责是什么？你眼中的成功是什么？你最大的愿景和梦想是什么？” （00:55:25）这样你就能更清楚上下文，从而助力自己的职业发展。反之，如果你说：“经理，这些是我的愿景和梦想。我擅长这项技能，但不确定升职副总裁需要具备哪些条件。你能给我指点迷津吗？” （00:55:45）这样的对话同样宝贵，因为你能获得全面的信息，进而决定是否要推进目标。若有决心，就向经理寻求帮助：“如果你发现有机会能提升我的演讲能力或沟通技巧，请告诉我。” 甚至更主动地说：“如果您对我的沟通能力有改进建议，我很乐意听取，因为这正是我提升这项技能的关键。”（00:56:11）如此一来，合作关系就能从对抗转为共赢，避免出现“我逼你升职，你逼我加班”的恶性循环。
