turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Feedback is one of the other topics that I am super, duper passionate about. And my general impression for both myself, everyone I've worked with, is that we don't value feedback enough or we don't think about it enough. Again, companies have these performance cycles, and so we're all like, yes, every six months we're going to go and do these reviews. That's when I'll get feedback. But feedback really, in my mind, ideally, should be a daily practice. Because the thing that matters for us in the long run as a team is how quickly are we getting better? So a team that just gets 1% better every week compared to a team that gets 1% better a month, even if they start off at a much lower baseline, is going to outperform in a very short amount of time the team that doesn't get better. (00:58:50): And so, what is the best tool for us to get better? It is feedback. And what I think about in feedback, it's very similar to what we said earlier about data metrics. It's essentially trying to put your hypotheses and test them against reality. So as an example, maybe I have this perception right now that I am a positive and engaging speaker. So, I have this sense that I'm smiling and I'm very engaging, and I'm telling great stories, but is that really true? I don't know. The reality is that I'm often biased, and we know these psychological effects where sometimes the Dunning-Kruger effect, people think they're way more expert at something than they actually are. You ask people, "Hey, are you a better than average driver?" (00:59:35): And it's like 70 or 80% of people, "Yes, I'm better than average." (00:59:38): How could that possibly be? We have biases. And imposter syndrome is a bias on the other side, it's like me feeling, "Oh, I suck. I don't actually belong here." Whereas, that also is a bias. It may not actually be true. In fact, I might very well be here and other people value my contribution. (00:59:56): So we are just wildly out of sync a lot of times in our perceptions of ourselves, our strengths, our weaknesses, what's going on. And the way that we're going to understand and truly get better is we need other people to reflect back what is actually their truth. And the way I think about it is like, I'm going to ask you for feedback after this podcast episode and you're going to tell me something. And what you're going to do is you're going to give me a gift. Because it'll be a gift of reflecting something back of what you see that I can't see. Just like if I have a leaf in the back of my head, I can't see that. And so if you're telling me, "Hey, Julie, you have a leaf." (01:00:33): "Oh, wow, thank you." Okay, maybe I can get rid of the leaf or whatnot. But that is what feedback is. It is essentially reflection back. It helps us calibrate to reality, and it allows me to get this information about whether or not I'm moving in the direction of my goals.
turns.zh:
反馈是我极其热衷的话题之一。就我个人以及我合作过的每个人的经验而言，我们对反馈的重视程度远远不够，或者说我们对反馈的思考不够深入。企业通常会设定绩效周期，然后大家都会觉得，好，每六个月我们就要进行评估，届时才能得到反馈。但在我看来，理想的反馈应该是一种日常实践。因为从长远来看，对团队最重要的是我们能否快速提升。例如，一支每周仅进步1%的团队，与一支每月进步1%的团队相比，即便后者起点低得多，最终也必然会在短期内超越停滞不前的前者。

（00:58:50）那么，获得改进的最佳工具是什么？答案就是反馈。反馈与我们之前讨论的数据指标非常相似，本质上就是验证假设并对照现实。举个例子，我现在可能认为自己是一个积极且善于互动的演讲者。我觉得自己面带微笑、充满活力，还能讲精彩的故事，但这真的属实吗？我不确定。现实是我们常有偏见，比如丹宁-克鲁格效应（Dunning-Kruger effect），人们会高估自己的能力。当你问别人：“你觉得自己开车比平均水平好吗？”（00:59:35），80%的人会回答：“是的，我比平均水平强。” （00:59:38）但这怎么可能呢？我们有偏见。自卑症（imposter syndrome）也是另一种偏见，让人觉得自己一无是处，不配待在这里。然而这同样是偏见，可能并非事实。事实上，我很可能能力出众，别人也很重视我的贡献。

（00:59:56）因此，我们对自己的认知、优势、弱点以及所处环境的理解往往存在巨大偏差。要真正理解并改进自己，就需要他人反馈真实情况。以我为例，我会在本期播客结束后征求反馈，而你们的反馈对我来说就是一份礼物。它能让我看到自己看不到的盲区，就如同后脑勺长叶子般难以察觉。当你告诉我“朱莉，你头上长叶子了”，（01:00:33）“哇，谢谢。”或许我能及时摘掉那片叶子。但这就是反馈的本质——反馈本身就是一种反思。它帮助我们与现实对标，让我获取是否朝着目标前进的信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I completely agree. The challenge for most people, as you know, is giving feedback that people receive and don't feel defensive about, and then receiving feedback and not being like, "Oh, no, they don't know. They don't know anything. How dare they say this about me?" (01:01:06): Could you give us maybe a tip or two for delivering feedback well and for receiving feedback well? And maybe even just seeking, how do you get more feedback? This all makes a lot of sense. Most of the time people don't get any feedback.
turns.zh: 我太认同了。大多数人的挑战在于，既要给出对方能接受且不产生防御心理的反馈，又要坦然接受反馈而不感到被攻击。比如，“哦，不，他们根本不懂。他们什么都不懂。他们怎么敢这么说我？”（01:01:06）能否给我们一些给出高质量反馈和接受反馈的建议？甚至是如何主动寻求反馈的技巧？这一切都很有道理。但大多数人根本得不到反馈。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: The best way... The first tip on getting feedback or delivering hard feedback is first go and actually establish that our relationship is one in which we value each other's contribution, we want to help each other grow, and therefore we're going to be the kind of people that want to give feedback to each other every week. So when you first start working with someone, don't wait until something bad has happened [inaudible 01:01:42] given feedback, because that's already a pressurized situation. Start by saying, "Hey, really excited to work with you. I feel like our best collaboration is I want you to help me get better. I think I'm good at this stuff. I'm not so good at this stuff. What about you? Okay, you think you're good at this stuff? How about we just work together and we just help each other get better at these things? And the way we're going to do that is, all feedback is open. I want you to tell me everything. Ideally, you're going to then say, 'Yeah, I want you to tell me everything.'" And we've already established that.
turns.zh: 获取反馈或提供建设性反馈的最佳方法……首先要建立这样一种关系：我们重视彼此的贡献，愿意帮助彼此成长。因此，我们要成为每周都愿意互相给予反馈的人。所以当你刚开始与某人合作时，别等到出了问题才去反馈——那时往往已处于高压状态。可以先说：“嘿，真的很高兴能与你共事。对我来说，我们最理想的合作方式是，你能帮助我提升自己。我觉得自己在某些方面做得不错，但有些方面还需要改进。你呢？你觉得自己在哪些方面擅长？不如我们携手合作，共同提升彼此的能力吧？”而实现这一目标的关键在于，所有反馈都必须公开透明。我希望你能毫无保留地告诉我你的想法。理想情况下，你会回应：“没错，我愿意随时向你反馈。”而这种信任感早已建立起来了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is colleagues or manager or all colleagues?
turns.zh: 那适用于同事、上司还是所有人呢？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: It's like everyone. It's like people you're dating, it's like your children. It can be with everyone, just establishing what kind of relationship do we want to have? I think most people want to opt into a relationship where you can be close, you can be tight with one another. You can say things to one another and not have to hide behind... I think most people will opt into it, and if you opt into it, everything gets easier down the road. So the first thing is get everyone to opt in that this is the kind of relationship that we want to have.
turns.zh: 适用于所有人。无论是恋人、孩子，还是同事，都可以如此。关键在于明确我们希望建立怎样的关系。我相信大多数人都渴望建立亲密、紧密的合作关系，能够坦诚交流，不必藏着掖着。这样一来，反馈过程就会更加顺畅。因此，首要任务是让每个人都认同这种合作模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One trickle throughout that I've heard that worked really well along these same lines is asking people, "Do you prefer feedback in the moment or do you prefer it kind of every month or every week or something like that?" (01:02:53): And everyone's like, "No, no in the moment and just tell me as soon as something happens." (01:02:57): And then that gives you that freedom to just, " Okay, yeah, let me give you feedback here."
turns.zh:
我听说过一个行之有效的小技巧：询问对方：“你更希望即时反馈，还是每月、每周等定期反馈？”（01:02:53）  
几乎所有人都回答：“不，我希望即时反馈，一有问题就直接说。”（01:02:57）  
这样一来，你就能自由地说：“好的，那我现在就给你反馈。”

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: So if you get people to opt in, "Yes, I want us to have a great relationship. I want us to help each other get better. I want feedback." That's 60% of the hard part of delivering difficult feedback later on. (01:03:13): Then the second tactic I will say is that when you actually give the feedback, it helps a lot. First, you have to check, "Am I actually giving this feedback because it's in the spirit of trying to help one another?" And if the answer is yes, then we've moved from 60% to 80%, it's going to go well. (01:03:37): But what can often happen is something happens. You do something, it triggers me, because I don't know, I had a bad experience about that type of thing before. And so, I'm kind of feeling mad and I want to be right. If my real rationale for why I want to give you feedback is I want to validate myself, I want to be right, I want to tell you you're wrong, I want to punish you, it's not going to go well. It's just already there. There's no way you can deliver it, unless you're a tremendous actor. It's just not going to go well. So you have to first check your intention. (01:04:16): But if you've done that, you're like, "No, no, no. I thought about it. I'm calm now. I'm not seeing red. I really think that Lenny is just not aware that when he says this, it makes me and other people feel left out," or whatever it is, right? Then I need to be able to give it to you. (01:04:33): And so usually then if you're like, "Okay, now I might be nervous because I don't want to offend you. I really value our relationship. How am I going to tell you. I don't want you to get defensive?" (01:04:44): Then the third tactic is, just say that out loud. If I sit down with you and I say, "Lenny, I'm so nervous right now. I want to give you some feedback and I'm really worried that it's going to impact our relationship, and I so value our relationship and I don't want that to happen. But I also feel like it's just going to help you to hear it if you can." (01:05:06): That does so much of the work of... It's humanizing. You're going to realize that I'm going out on the limb, I'm being really vulnerable, and likely you're going to hear that so much more than if I just find a way to drop it, just lobby it over because it's so difficult. Just actually lean into the fact that it is difficult and expose that because that builds a lot of human connection.
turns.zh:
因此，如果你能让对方主动接受反馈，说：“是的，我希望我们能建立良好的关系。我希望我们能互相帮助进步。我希望得到反馈。” 这就完成了传递困难反馈的60%工作。（01:03:13）  
接下来，我要说的第二个策略是，当你真正给出反馈时，要确保动机正确。首先，你得检查：“我给出这个反馈，是出于真心想帮助对方吗？”如果答案是肯定的，那么成功率就会从60%提升到80%，沟通就能顺利进行。（01:03:37）  
但有时可能会出现意外状况。比如，你做了某件事，却触发了对方的情绪，因为对方之前有过类似的负面经历。这时，你可能会感到愤怒，急于证明自己是对的，想指责对方。这时候，传递反馈的目的就偏离了初衷，沟通注定失败。除非你是个天生的演员，否则很难挽救局面。  
所以，你首先要审视自己的动机。（01:04:16）  
但如果经过反思，你能意识到：“不，不不。我冷静下来了。我没有生气。我真的认为莱尼没有意识到，他说那些话会让我和其他人感到被排斥。” 这时候，你就需要把这些想法清晰地传达出来。（01:04:33）  
第三个策略是，大胆说出自己的担忧。比如，你可以坦诚地说：“莱尼，我现在很紧张。我想给你反馈，但又担心这会影响我们的关系。我很珍惜我们之间的情谊，不想因此失去你。但我觉得如果你能虚心听取反馈，肯定会有帮助。” （01:05:06）  
这样做能有效化解矛盾。你的真诚会打动对方，让他们更容易接受你的建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is amazing advice. Very tactical. Okay, is there anything else? So we've talked about a bunch of timeless pieces of manager wisdom, things that people need to hear, especially as new managers. Is there anything else that you think is really important that you think people are just not fully grokking for being great managers?
turns.zh: 这些建议真是太棒了。非常实用。有没有其他要补充的吗？我们已经讨论了很多经久不衰的管理智慧，对新晋管理者来说尤其重要。还有哪些你认为人们需要深刻领会的管理要领呢？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I think the idea of win-win, I think about that all the time in my mind. And I go back to it, because I think that often we have the story in our heads that sometimes things are adversarial. As a manager, I'm trying to get people to be more productive, so I'm trying to get them to do a thing that maybe they don't want to do. I'm going to try and get them to work harder or I'm going to somehow put more pressure on them. If you start thinking like that, that's not a win-win way to be thinking, right? That's like you saying, "My getting better outcomes has to come at the expense of somebody else losing something." (01:06:33): And I think if you start thinking like that, it's very difficult to come up with a strategy or to truly be successful. But if you say, "Look, actually, my job is to figure out how to create win-wins." So I actually don't want somebody over the long run to feel like what I've done is just create a ton of pressure for them and now they're super burnt out, real quick, because that's not good for our team, that's not good for me, that's not good for our long-term relationship. How do we find the solution that can be a win-win? And I think if you think like that, a lot of things get easier. So for example, with new managers, I think this is true for me, too, the first time I had to tell someone that they shouldn't be a part of this team was extremely fraught for me. And the main reason was because I'm putting myself in their shoes, and I'm imagining that this is truly horrible, and I've just done a huge disservice to this person, and that's the most awful thing. (01:07:32): But there's another way to look at it, which is, hey, if there's persons on the team, they probably want to be successful. They want to do great work, they want to be valued, they want to grow their career. If this is not the place for them, because it doesn't align with their true interests and the things that are going to help them be successful is just not the thing that they either want to do or can do at this point, it doesn't do that person any good for me to somehow try to continue to make it. It's actually going to be miserable. I'm going back to prolonging that misery state. (01:08:06): And so, sometimes a win-win thing is to just say, "Look, it's not working, and I respect and value you so much that I know you want to do something that you can be proud of and you can grow in, and that's going to be really valued. And right here, what we got, this isn't it." (01:08:22): That's like a win-win way of looking at the situation, not a like, "Oh, my firing them is just definitely going to be a horrible..." (01:08:31): I'm not trying to say it's not going to be hard, obviously it's hard, but it's in the mentality and the mental model I think makes all the difference. Because it's going to be different in the way that I convey it to them. It's going to be different and why this actually in the grander scheme of things may be great, and it's going to reduce this adversarial feeling where they're now going to see me as an enemy or somebody with all this power who's making choices that impact them and they feel powerless. It has to be a collaboration. And I think if it's not win-win... And I could be wrong. I would say I don't think it's right. The person could actually say, "No, you're wrong." And that would actually be great information, because then maybe we can go back and we can find a way to make it win-win.
turns.zh:
我认为"双赢"的理念，我一直在心里反复思考。我反复回归这个概念，因为我觉得人们常常陷入一种对抗性思维模式。作为管理者，我试图让员工更高效地工作，这意味着我可能要让他们去做一些他们不愿做的事。我会试图让他们更努力工作，或者给他们施加更大压力。如果你这样想，这就不是双赢的思维方式，对吧？这就像在说"我要获得更好的结果，就必须以他人失去为代价"。（01:06:33）  
我认为，如果你这样想，就很难制定出成功的策略或取得真正的成功。但如果你换个角度思考，"看，其实我的工作就是想办法创造双赢局面"。那么从长远来看，我不希望有人因为我的做法而感到压力巨大、身心俱疲，因为这对团队、对我自己、对我们的长期合作关系都没有好处。我们该如何找到双赢的解决方案？我觉得这样想，很多事情就会变得容易得多。  
例如，对新晋管理者来说，我自己也深有体会。第一次不得不告知某人他们不适合加入团队时，我内心无比煎熬。主要原因是我设身处地为他们着想，觉得这太残酷了，自己对这个人造成了巨大的伤害，这是最糟糕的。  
但另一种看法是，嘿，如果团队中有这样的人，他们肯定希望成功。他们想做出出色的工作，渴望被重视，渴望职业发展。如果这里不适合他们，因为这与他们的真正兴趣不符，而帮助他们成功的因素恰恰是他们目前不想做或无法做到的，那就强行留下只会让他们痛苦不堪。我这是在延续痛苦的状态。  
所以有时候双赢的做法就是坦然地说：“看，这行不通，我非常尊重和重视你，我知道你想做令自己自豪、能成长的事，这会得到认可。而我们现在的情况显然不符合。”  
这才是双赢的思维方式，而不是“哦，解雇他们肯定很糟糕……”  
（01:08:31）  
我不是说这不难，显然很难，但我认为这种思维模式和心态才是关键。因为我传达给他们的方式会不同。这种方式会让他们更容易接受，实际上从大局来看可能更有利，也能减少对抗感——他们不会把我视为敌人，或者视为一个掌握着生杀大权、任意做决定的人。必须是合作共赢。如果不是双赢……我可能错了。但我觉得这是不对的。对方可能会说：“不，你错了。” 那这其实也是很好的信息，因为这样我们就能回过头来，找到双赢的解决之道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was just going to say, they have to believe this. You can't just make it sound like this, "Here's the win you're getting let go. It's a huge win for you." But in reality, the way you phrased it, it is actually almost always true, "This is just not a place that you'll be happy and succeed at, and it's better you go do something else."
turns.zh: 是啊，我正想说呢，他们得相信这一点。你不能只说得好像这样，"这是你被裁掉的胜利。这对你们来说是个巨大的胜利。"但实际上，按照你刚才的表述，情况往往恰恰相反，"这里不是你能快乐成功的地方，你最好去做点别的。"

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm going to keep fishing in this pool to see what else we got, but when we run out, let me know. Is there anything else that you think people should know, should hear, especially new managers that they're still not fully getting?
turns.zh: 好的。我要继续在这池子里捞一捞，看看还有什么其他收获，但如果没得捞了，记得告诉我。还有什么你觉得人们应该知道、应该听听的，尤其是那些新晋管理者，他们可能还没完全领会的？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I think being aware of your own energy and conviction is really, really important. So a lot of these themes, as you can see, go back to, you have to first understand this about yourself and have the right mindset, and when you do, it becomes much easier to be able to be impactful with other people. So this is another one. I think it's very difficult for managers to be able... We talked a lot about the three pillars of what are the major tools of a manager. The first is people. And so, we talked a lot about the importance of dimensionality and feedback and helping reflect and grow people. (01:10:21): I think the second one is around purpose. Purpose is like, "What are we here to do? What's our North Star?" (01:10:28): And I think it's very hard to actually convey that if you don't have conviction yourself. And so watching your conviction is really important, particularly since a lot of people who are managers, you often start out not as the founder of the CEO of the company, but you might be a middle manager. So in some ways, you didn't create the vision, but you are in some ways expected to execute it or take a piece of it and do it. And I find that sometimes what new managers don't pay attention to enough is what is their true belief. They feel like they might have to be a soldier, so they just get orders and they have to execute it. But it really makes a difference if they themselves have gone through the work of thinking through, "Wait, why are we doing this? Do I believe this strategy? Does it make sense or not?" (01:11:18): And if it doesn't make sense, to go and actually have the conversation with their manager or whoever else, just so they can get to alignment on, "I really believe in what I'm doing." (01:11:29): Because if you don't really believe in what you're doing or you're just parroting the thing that got passed through the organization, it's very hard for you to then be able to help other people see what that magic is or to be actually really effective as a person who can hold that vision and that purpose. So I just think you have to really check in with yourself on like, "Wait, I know we're told to do this and this is what we have to do, but how do we really feel about it?" (01:11:56): Because if you don't feel good about it, then it's not going to be very likely that the project's going to succeed. I can tell you right now, every single manager I've ever managed where they're like, "I don't really think this is a good idea," there's no case where I can think of where the project somehow turned out to be wildly successful.
turns.zh: 我觉得意识到自己的能量和信念真的非常非常重要。所以你可以看到，很多主题都回归到，你首先要理解自己的这一点，要有正确的心态。当你做到这一点后，就能更轻松地对他人产生影响。这又是一个重点。我觉得管理者要做到这一点非常难。我们谈了很多管理者的三大工具。第一个是人。所以我们谈了很多维度、反馈以及帮助人们反思和成长的重要性。（01:10:21）：我觉得第二个是关于目标。目标就是，“我们来这里是为了做什么？我们的北极星是什么？” （01:10:28）：我觉得如果自己没有信念的话，其实很难真正传达出这个目标。所以观察自己的信念真的很重要，尤其是因为很多成为管理者的人，一开始不是公司的创始人或CEO，而是中层管理者。某种程度上，你不是创造愿景的人，但你却被期望去执行它，或者拿走一部分去实现它。我发现新晋管理者有时不太注意自己的真实信念。他们觉得自己可能得当个士兵，所以只接受命令然后执行。但如果他们自己花时间思考过，“等等，我们为什么要这么做？我相信这个策略吗？它有没有道理？” （01:11:18）：如果没有道理，就去和经理或其他人沟通，确保达成一致，"我真的相信自己在做的事。" （01:11:29）：因为如果你自己都不相信自己在做的事，或者只是在重复公司传下来的东西，那你就很难真正帮助别人看到其中的魔力，或者真正高效地成为一个能坚守愿景和目标的人。所以我觉得你真的得审视自己，"等等，我们被告知要做这个，要做那个，但我们对此感觉如何？" （01:11:56）：因为如果你感觉不好的话，这个项目就不太可能成功。我可以告诉你，我管理过的每个管理者，如果他们说"我不觉得这是个好主意"，我都想不出有哪一个项目最后取得了巨大的成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such a classic challenge of managers, is getting things done that you don't really agree with. And I can't help but ask you for advice on someone that isn't in that place of just, "Okay, we have this feature our CEO's prioritizing. This is not a good idea, but I need to have a brave face and not make it sound like I'm just being told what to do and I'm just reporting orders. I don't believe in this." You don't want to do that. You become a terrible unsuccessful manager and people lose trust in you. What's your advice to folks that are in that place of just how to find that balance?
turns.zh: 这确实是管理者面临的一个经典挑战——当你不得不去做一些自己并不认同的事情时。我不禁想请教你一个问题：当有人并非处于那种“好吧，总裁优先考虑这个功能，虽然我觉得这不是个好主意，但我得强装镇定，不让别人觉得我在被指挥行事”的境地时，该如何找到平衡？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: So I think, first, if you feel that way, you got to actually find a way to get it out and engage in dialogue. So if you're like, "My manager told me to do this, I think it's a terrible idea," you've got to talk to your manager about it or you've got to talk to the CEO or whoever and feel... Because once you engage in a dialogue, what will often happen is you'll learn more, you'll have new information, you'll have new assumptions, and maybe you'll have influenced a project in some manner. But often, the more you can learn about, "Okay, why did some other smart people feel like we should do this? And what parts of it do I believe and what parts am I more skeptical about?" (01:13:20): You can probably decompose it from a blanket it's good or bad to like, "Okay, this is a hypothesis, this is a hypothesis, this is a hypothesis. I might kind of believe this one. The reason I don't like the proposal, I don't believe this particular hypothesis, but I believe these other ones." (01:13:36): And so, when you can start to get one level deeper into breaking it down into a set of assumptions, that makes it much easier, because then likely find something that you do kind of resonate with. And you might be able to then steer things like, "Okay, if that hypothesis doesn't... I believe in disagree and commit, but now we can be very specific. We can isolate the thing that..." (01:13:59): And what we can also often do is like, "Okay, the reason I didn't like this proposal is because I believe that this assumption is wrong." (01:14:07): I'm going to come up with a really stupid example. But your suggestion is, "I know we have a great idea. We're going to go and put a lemonade stand on every block. And my core assumption is people do not like lemonade. That's not the hot beverage right now. And so therefore, I think this is a stupid plan." (01:14:25): But if I talk to you about it and you're like, "No, no, this is the core assumption we disagree on." (01:14:29): Likely what starts to unfold is like, "Well, can we get some data? Can we get some information? Is there a quicker way to validate whether people like lemonade? Perhaps we should just test it in one market before we go and open up the lemonade stands across the entire 50 states." (01:14:45): And so what happens is we can likely get to the actual specific area and come up with something. And then, if I have to now share with my team, We're going to try this hypothesis. I'm not sure how I feel about it, but I actually do think... I don't know for sure and our CEO seems to think this is... But we're just going to test it."
turns.zh:
所以我认为，如果你有这种感受，就必须想办法把它表达出来，进行对话。比如，如果你说：“经理让我做这个，我觉得这主意糟透了。”你得和经理谈谈，或者找CEO或其他高层聊聊，坦诚自己的想法。因为一旦开启对话，你往往能获得更多信息，重新审视问题，也许还能对项目产生影响。关键在于，你要从一概而论的“这主意好还是坏”，逐步拆解成一系列假设。比如：“好吧，这是一个假设，这个假设，这个假设。我可能比较认同这个假设。但我不认同这个提案，因为我不相信这个特定假设，但我相信其他假设。”（01:13:20）

当你能更深入地拆解假设时，事情会变得容易得多，因为你很可能能找到自己认同的部分。然后你就能引导讨论：“好吧，如果这个假设不成立……我认同‘不同意并执行’的原则，但现在我们可以更具体地讨论。我们可以把问题锁定在……” （01:13:59）

我们还常会这样做：“好吧，我不喜欢这个提案是因为我认为这个假设有误。” （01:14:07）

我举个极端的例子：你说：“我知道我们有个绝佳的主意，要在每个街区开设柠檬水摊。我的核心假设是人们不喜欢柠檬水，它现在可不是热门饮品。所以我觉得这计划很蠢。” （01:14:25）

但如果你和我讨论这个问题，你可能会说：“不不，这才是我们争执的核心假设。” （01:14:29）

接下来可能的讨论会是：“那我们能收集些数据吗？能获取些信息吗？有没有更快的方法验证人们是否喜欢柠檬水？或许我们应该先在一个市场测试，再决定是否在全美50个州推广。” （01:14:45）

最终我们能找到具体的切入点，制定行动方案。比如：“现在我得和团队分享这个假设。我不确定是否认同，但我确实觉得……我不确定，但CEO似乎认为……不过我们还是先测试看看。”

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: For sure, and our CEO seems to think this is... But we're just going to test it, and we're going to do the test in a way where... That's what we want to find out, is do 18 to 25-year-olds love lemonade if we put them on these neighborhood college campuses? It becomes very specific and everyone's like, "Well, yeah, I don't know for sure, but I'm happy to go in, and test that, and commit to it."
turns.zh: 确实，我们的CEO似乎也这么认为……但我们只需进行测试，并且要以一种……的方式来开展测试。我们想知道的是，如果把18至25岁的年轻人带到大学校园里，他们会不会喜欢柠檬水呢？这就变得非常具体了，大家都会说：“嗯，我不确定，但我很乐意参与测试并为此付出努力。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such a good advice, and there's also, you could layer on, "Here's the things I do agree with and believe. Here's the ways that I see this as totally right. Here's the piece that I'm not so sure about, but that's why we're going to run this test, and here's why it's the smallest version of this test and why it's a great idea just to figure it out." We'll show them. You probably don't want to say that. As you give this answer, it's so interesting, I almost want to do a whole new episode with you later of just common conundrums managers have, challenges that every manager runs into that are really difficult to figure out on the spot. We could save that for the future. Okay, I'm going to take us to a couple of recurring themes on this podcast, occasional recurring that every episode corners that we take guests to. (01:16:07): The first is I want to take us to AI corner. turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I believe that there's infinity in every direction. That makes me pretty contrarian on pretty much everything that anyone says. If someone says something like on Twitter, I sometimes play this game with myself, which is in what context would that actually not be true? I think the reality is that the world is so, or at least my reality and my understanding of the reality, is that the world is just infinitely complex. For example, if my kids say something like going outside is boring, or taking a walk is boring, or doing something is boring, my general response will be, "Well, it's because you're not seeing the infinity that's in that direction." (01:21:05): Even, for example, something really mundane like staring at a blank wall, I think that you can make that actually deeply, deeply interesting, because you can use that as an opportunity to go into your own mind and to figure out how you can make time pass, or you can meditate on the existence or meditate on your breath, or just be grateful for the purpose of being alive. Two people, one person you can say, "Sit in front of a wall for an hour," and, like my kid, they will super complain and be like, "This is the worst thing ever," but you can put somebody else like a monk and they'll have a wonderful experience. It's not really about the environment or the wall. It's really about how we see it and whether we can find the thing that is deep, and rich, and infinite in that direction.
turns.zh: 我相信每个方向都存在无穷无尽的事物。这让我对别人说的大多数话都持有相反的看法。比如有人在推特上发言时，我有时会自问："这种说法在什么情况下才不成立呢？"我认为现实世界——至少对我而言——就是无比复杂的。比如，当我的孩子们说"出去玩很无聊"、"散步很无聊"或者"做任何事都无聊"时，我的回应通常是："那是因为你没有看到那个方向的无限可能性。"（01:21:05）：即便是一些看似平常的事，比如盯着空白的墙壁，我也认为只要善加利用，就能让它变得极其有趣。你可以借此深入自己的内心世界，思考如何消磨时间，或者静坐冥想，感恩生命的存在。面对同样的环境，两个人的反应截然不同。一个孩子可能会抱怨"这是最糟糕的事"，而修行者却能从中获得美妙的体验。这其实无关环境本身，而在于我们如何看待它，以及能否在其中发现无穷无尽的深度与丰富性。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: The first is Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance. I absolutely love that book. It's beautifully written. It's so deep. My whole philosophy around quality is beautifully... A lot of it comes from that book, the idea and even all the stuff that we talked about change. What does it mean to be at that forefront of change and dynamic quality? I think he just talks about so beautifully and so masterfully in that book. Old classic, but I try to reread it every few years or so. Second is Conscious Business. It is my favorite management book. It's a little bit of a sleeper head because I actually end up recommending this one far more than my own book.
turns.zh: 第一本是《禅与摩托车维修艺术》。我特别喜欢这本书。文字优美，思想深刻。我对品质的整个理念都深受其影响，很多观点都源自这本书，比如变革前沿和动态品质的含义。我觉得他在这本书里把这些都讲得极其美妙、极其高明。是本经典之作，但我每隔几年都会重读一遍。第二本是《意识商业》。这是我最喜欢的管理学著作。这本书有点被低估，因为我推荐它的次数远超推荐自己的书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哇哦。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I read this one after I wrote my book, and I always tell people that if I read it before, I'm not sure I would've written my book, because I would've been like, "Conscious Business is really the book that really, really so much resonates." Many of the things I talked about, this idea of win-win, idea of being a player, not a victim, and how to think about work, not just it's a job but how do you really think about aligning it with your own personal values and what you want to do in the world, I think that this book really speaks to that so beautifully. It is also very tactical. It's got a lot of really wonderful examples. I will tell people, the cover isn't very attractive, and I think that if you judge a book by its cover, this seems very corporate-y. The title also seems like, "What conscious business?" and the first chapter is a little bit more technical. But if you just get past it and get into chapter two and you start with examples of the soccer team, it's just the best management book.
turns.zh: 我写完书后读了这本书，我常跟人说，如果我之前读了这本书，可能就不会写那本《意识商业》了，因为我会想：“《意识商业》这本书真是太有共鸣了。” 我谈到的很多理念，比如双赢思维、不要做受害者而要做参与者，以及如何看待工作——不只是份工作，而是如何与个人价值观和理想事业相契合——我觉得这本书把这些讲得太好了。它也很实用，里面有很多精彩案例。我会告诉别人，封面不太吸引人，如果以貌取书的话，这本书看起来很商业化。书名也让人有点费解，第一章还有点技术性。但只要跳过第一章，进入第二章，从足球队的例子开始讲起，这就是最棒的管理学著作了。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yes. Okay, third book. I love the book Good Inside by Dr. Becky. Yes, you can use AI to do that, but really, don't think about it as a shortcut tool, because if that's the case, I don't actually think that they're going to be able to become the kind of people they want to be in the world.
